item.title: Where is all the AI safety research uplift?
item.description:
(Thanks to @Goutham Nalagatla for discussion and for sitting with me and talking about it while I wrote it.)

METR recently released a report estimating that Anthropic is getting an overall 1.7x acceleration in AI capability progress as a result of AI accelerating their work. As many have noted (see e.g. Ajeya’s post), this 1.7x acceleration implies that research is being sped up by much more than 1.7x; Ajeya speculates 10x (which is similar to the ~12x uplift estimated by Anthropic staff).  That is, this result implies that researchers are producing about 10 times as many quality-adjusted results as they would without AI progress, or as they were a year or two ago.

Anthropic researchers estimated that Mythos 5 caused 5x uplift, and we have access to Opus 5.5, which is somewhat better. (I didn’t take their estimate that seriously at the time, because it was quite unclear how the estimate was produced and it seemed very surprising (see Ryan’s discussion at the time), but I’m taking it more seriously now as a result of it being consistent with the METR report).

If this is the case, then AIs speed up AI safety research as much as AI capabilities research, we might expect Anthropic safety researchers to be working 10x faster, and external safety researchers to be working 5x faster now and 10x faster soon.

And external safety researchers can probably scale compute use faster than Anthropic capabilities researchers can. For example, we at Redwood are well-funded and would totally 5x our compute spend if we had 5x as many experiments to run, unlike Anthropic capabilities researchers who are presumably already doing a pretty good job of using all the compute they have. So I think that we should expect a 5x labor acceleration to turn into more like a 5x research project acceleration.

I don't think our empirical research has been going 5x faster since we got access to Fable/Opus 5.5; I would have guessed more like 2-3x speedup. Why is this?

  •  Maybe we suck and have not adopted AI as effectively as Anthropic capabilities researchers have.
    • This might be the case. Obviously, Redwood researchers extensively use AI agents for their research, mostly using Claude Code and recently Claude Tag. We also have an in-house scaffold for autonomous AI research, which has produced results that we've published in the past (e.g. here, here), though we haven't put a lot of work into using or improving this scaffold in the last few months.
      • We found that this research scaffold is pretty good at doing empirical research, but Claude sometimes makes extremely unhinged choices that invalidate its results and is also pretty bad at writing up its findings; these weaknesses substantially reduced how quickly we could use it to produce useful research outputs.
    • If Anthropic had scaffolds that made their models drastically more useful, I expect they would have turned them into products?
      • Maybe they get a lot of uplift from Anthropic-specific infra for their AIs?
      • Maybe they don’t release scaffold features that are specifically useful for ML research?
    • Overall, I think this is maybe a partial explanation, but it seems sort of surprising for our uplift to be way smaller than Anthropic’s. It’s really felt like fundamental weaknesses of the models, rather than scaffold limitations, are the main reason that they haven’t been more useful to us.
  • To some extent, our work is probably less accelerated by AI than Anthropic capabilities research is.
    • I think most of our empirical research is similarly well-suited to AI speedup to most published ML capabilities research.
    • Maybe Anthropic capabilities research is particularly well suited to AI speedup compared to most ML research? Some of the pretraining work may rely more on the AI's strengths. This could be the case if, for example, a big blocker on running experiments on new architectures is implementing them efficiently.
      • One person from Anthropic told me recently that they think that capabilities research is notably more sped up than most of their short-term alignment work.
  • Maybe we've become much more bottlenecked on research judgment, and I haven't noticed? A lot of the research we do is conducted by interns or relatively junior staff who work fairly closely with their manager to prioritize future experiments. Maybe it's the case that our IC researchers are, in fact, going way faster, but this just means they're much more bottlenecked by their managers' time to understand what they're up to.
    • And maybe this is more true of us vs Anthropic because more of their ICs are more senior/self-reliant, or their research requires less tricky judgement?

There are some cases where huge speedup happened. E.g. my guess is that Ryan’s work in the Hugging Face investigation was made wildly faster through his intense use of AI agents; this speedup was partially due to the project being pretty amenable to massive agent use (because it involved reading lots of stuff) and partially due to Ryan being experienced with insane agent workflows.

Whatever the case is, I feel like we are imminently going to learn a lot about how feasible it is to accelerate AI safety research using AI labor. If empirical AI safety is going to be drastically sped up by AI, that should translate into a huge increase in the rate of valuable outputs from external AI safety researchers very soon. At the very least, if we don’t see huge speedups on the kind of AI safety work that is most amenable to huge speedups, I’m going to think the researchers doing that work are doing something wrong.

See also AI speeds up 3rd party safety researchers by ~1.6x (via self-reports)

item.title: Ajeya: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research right now
item.description:
Earlier this week, Anthropic stated in their S1 that they “may imminently meet” the threshold of “dramatically accelerated progress due to AI” as defined in their Responsible Scaling Policy. In their latest RSP (effective July 2026), say this threshold will be met when:

  1. They observe or expect overall capabilities progress to be going twice as fast as the fastest sustained rate before AI was contributing much to AI R&D.
  2. This is plausibly attributable to AI automating AI R&D, rather than acceleration in compute or other inputs.

For the last few months, some of my colleagues at METR have been working on a deep-access investigation to understand how much Anthropic is being accelerated by its AI systems. From my reading of their report and Anthropic’s RSP, it looks like the “dramatic acceleration” threshold has already been crossed.

The report authors found that:

  1. Between October 2025 and October 2026, capabilities progress at Anthropic has been going about twice as fast as it had been over the previous twelve months. The measurement they report is an internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index called AECI; a wide range of other supporting evidence for acceleration has been redacted. They said that this redacted evidence was "a majority of the evidence [they] found most informative."
  2. While the pace may have initially started picking up for a mix of reasons, AI automation is probably the large majority of the reason why capabilities are still improving at this faster pace today. Their reasons for believing this have been redacted.

This is a much bigger deal than it might sound at first. I think this report is the most important update we have gotten about AI risk in the last couple of years — much bigger than the Hugging Face attack. Naively, it points toward much shorter timelines than most external researchers (including the AI 2027 team) have projected.

Importantly, if AI is roughly doubling capabilities progress overall, it must be speeding up human researchers by much more than that.

The rest of the post: https://www.planned-obsolescence.org/p/ai-is-dramatically-accelerating-ai

item.title: Notes on Take-Off Speeds and RSI
item.description:
I created these notes for use when I facilitate AI safety courses. I'm sharing these notes early because this issue is topical and I suspect it is better to make an imperfect version available early rather than a much more polished version available later.

Please note: some of this content was taken from Additional Course Context. I decided recently that the content on take-off speeds really belonged in the same document as the content on RSI, so I'll be releasing an new version of Additional Course Context at some point (to avoid spamming LW, it'll probably be Substack only; none of my work is paywalled). Some of the other content was taken from Notes on “We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety”. This Miles' article has been removed from the governance course, so I was looking for a new home for this content. I wanted to include it in a document that was intended to be shared in all the courses I facilitate.

Take-off Speed from Take-off Speeds Rules Everything Around Me:

Whilst there isn’t a strict definition of fast vs. slow takeoff, possibly the most influential definition comes from Paul Christiano (2018):

There will be a complete 4 year interval in which world output doubles, before the first 1 year interval in which world output doubles. (Similarly, we’ll see an 8 year doubling before a 2 year doubling, etc.)

At risk of oversimplifying, Paul argues that we should prima facie expect a slow takeoff because someone will generally figure out how to produce a “slightly worse” version of AI before someone figures out how to build the better version (he claims this is supported by the historical record of technological development overall).

Yudkowsky disagrees (2021), criticising the intuition that “design precursors with 95% of the technology should at least have 10% of the impact. He writes: "An awful lot of my model of deployment lag is adoption lag and regulatory lag and bureaucratic sclerosis across companies and countries” and “My mainline view is that growth stays at 5%/year and then everybody falls over dead in 3 seconds and the world gets transformed into paperclips"

How should we characterise progress up until now?

Eliezer recently wrote:

If Hanson or Christiano or Karnofsky etc etc believed this was what a "slow takeoff" looked like, they failed to convey that to their reassured, cheerful audience.

Tom Davidson responded:

If you thought this was what fast takeoff looked like, you also failed to convey that.

For reference, Eliezer previously defined a fast as meaning, “a timescale of weeks or hours rather than years or decades”.

“Bumpy” intelligence explosions

Forethought defines an additional scenario. For example, imagine if AI dramatically accelerates algorithm progress for a while, but then this plateaus whilst we figure out how to make robots that can automate the construction of chip fabs.

(Diagram note: the types of intelligence explosion will be explained in the next section)

In contrast, Arvind Narayanan (of AI as a Normal Technology) argues any RSI we do achieve will be narrow (that is jagged): ie. progress on verifiable tasks will continue “for a few more years” or even accelerate whilst progress on unverifiable tasks more or less remains “frustratingly hard”.

Richard Ngo also expects jaggedness to persist, as opposed to everything “going vertical”. Why? Because of a poorly understood “divergence” between “measured capabilities” and “real-world impacts” (nonetheless he asserts “things are going to look much weirder than almost anyone expects”):

Getting into the weeds

Whilst this is arguably less relevant these days, take-off speed is distinct from timelines. Take-off speeds are about how fast an intelligence explosion occurs if/when it happens whilst timelines are about when a particular milestone is achieved. Both slow-takeoff/short-timelines and fast-takeoff/long-timelines are conceptually possible.

Types of “Intelligence Explosion”:

Forethought examines three kinds of feedback loops:

Building on top of this, Forethought defines three kinds of intelligence explosion:

  1. software only recursive self-improvement
  2. AI-technology: driven by improvements in software and chip design,
  3. full-stack where AI also helps increase the production of chips.

The reason why each type of intelligence explosion includes the previous factors is that they’ve ordered the factors by expected lead-time. If an intelligence explosion is possible, fast takeoff vs. slow takeoff likely depends heavily on what kinds of intelligence explosion would be sufficiently powerful to trigger it. For example, a fast takeoff is much more likely where a software-only explosion is possible, however, if you need to automate the full-stack, then there’d be a much stronger argument for a slow takeoff.

Projecting trends into the future:

Tim Urban argues that, “it’s most intuitive for us to think linearly, when we should be thinking exponentially”

This forms a key crux: Can we project exponential trends into the future on the basis of induction (ie. the future being like the past) or is this foolish given that exponentials must end at some point? Development of most technologies has occurred as a series of s-curves (ie. sigmoids) which would support the latter view.

In contrast, Astralcodex points out that simply knowing that something is a sigmoid doesn’t tell you where you are on the curve (a hilarious graph from the World Energy Organisation shows them repeatedly, incorrectly predicting that exponential progress in terms of solar power will finish):

He also has a graph showing where researchers incorrectly predicted that the METR time horizons would cap out just as the curve zoomed upward):

Connor Leahry writes: “There are only two times to react to an exponential: Too early, or too late.” In many case this is true. However, early on it may be hard to know if it is an exponential or not. Unfortunately, in many cases we’ll just have to make such decisions under uncertainty.

Are we experiencing RSI?

  • Anthropic updated its S-1 form (for its IPO) with the following: “our internal estimates and our expectations regarding future models, rather than our current models, indicate that we may imminently meet our Responsible Scaling Policy’s definition of “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI” (click for their definition).
    • Jack Clarke had previously commented that it’s, “more likely (than not that) we’ll see full RSI become possible in 2027”
  • Independent METR report on Anthropic: “We believe that, as of Oct 2026, the pace of capability growth on well-specified tasks is likely about 2x what it was from Mar 2024 to Oct 2025. We’re highly uncertain and would not be surprised by 1.3x–3x.”.

(Source)

  • METR reports that their analysis significantly depends on analysis and evidence that Anthropic didn’t allow them to publish. However Karthik Tadepalli reports on their attempts to verify the report using public information (TLDR: the acceleration is real, AI is likely the cause, but its less clear how far we should expect this trend to continue)
  • Ryan Greenblatt estimates (based on his previous public comments to avoid any risk of revealing confidential info) an AI software R&D speed-up of 3.8x. The reason why this only results in a 2x speed-up in benchmark progress is because a) some increases in the scores comes from scaling compute (he estimates 2/3 of the progress comes from software improvements) b) there are decreasing marginal returns.
  • I’ve attached a diagram showing self-reported speedups. There’s likely significant selection effects here: employees might worry that they’d look bad if they reported less speed-up than others.
  • Key crux: to what extent do benchmark scores correspond to real world capabilities?
  • Apparently Sergey Brin is pushing Google to work towards recursive self-improvement to catch up to the frontier.
  • Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI contains a lot of interesting details on where we are with RSI.
  • I found the Anthropic self-improvement report less useful, though, like the OpenAI report it also showed their engineers shipping about 8 times as much code.
    • Limitations: This is a lot, but it’s hard to know how to correlate it with things that matter given how crude lines of code is as a measure. Engineers estimated the true output increase at 4 times. Of course, we might wonder how accurate subjective estimates actually are.
  • A P-Zero Research study into AI’s research taste found; “the experimental research taste of frontier models has doubled every ~3 months since December 2025. The best model, Opus 5.5, now exceeds our expert human baseline”.
    • Limitations: “Our results may overstate how fast research taste is improving. Our tasks are fast and cheap to verify, which frontier labs find easiest to hill-climb, and our human baseline doesn’t include top researchers, so it may significantly underestimate the performance of the best researchers in the world. TasteVal also doesn’t measure a model’s ability to choose which problems are most fruitful to work on.”

Are we sure?:

We’ll begin by considering two tables from DeepMind’s AGI to ASI which lays out potential bottlenecks and fundamental limitations of AI:

Toby Ord has argued that many people have failed to realise the implications of the shift from pre-training scaling to RL and inference-time scaling. A 100x increase in pre-training is equivalent to a 1,000x increase in inference or a 1,000,000x scale up of RL. He suggests that this effect has been masked since these factors hadn’t been scaled, but he suggests this is set to change with models already utilising significant inference-time compute and RL assigned a significant proportion of training compute (he has written a whole series on AI scaling).

Toby emphasises that METR wasn’t confidently able to rule out a one-time jump rather than an increase in slope. He performed a quick analysis using Opus which suggested that 1.4x is a better estimate of the new slope gradient than METR’s 1.9x.

Seb Krier shared graphs (generated with Claude) indicating that a linear increase in AECI requires an exponential increase in spending.

Tom Davidson points out that this might be viable because linear increases in ECI provide (in his view) exponential increases in productivity. Thus the outputs scale in the inputs.

AI as a normal technology argues that diffusion cycles provide a bottleneck. Specifically, in their model, it takes time for model capabilities to flow through to product changes and then for people to use them. This produces the data that we need for the next round of capabilities improvements and the dependency on data from deployment limits the speed of potential feedback loops:

Next we’ll consider Ramez Naam’s Where’s the “Intelligence Explosion”? which pushes back against the notion that we’ll encounter RSI any time soon. He argues that the current AI feedback loop is only 10-20% of the strength required. He interprets OpenAI internal automation data as showing the real world AI research is much harder than other benchmarks show. He further notes that Anthropic predicted a 40× speed up in researcher productivity would be required to double their rate of progress due to other bottlenecks.

This was published 27th Sep 2026, ie. before METR’s independent report on AI acceleration. It’ll be interesting to see his response:

https://x.com/ramez/status/2118472046812213577

If it does happen, how might it play out?

We’ll begin by naively projecting these trends forward:

Ajeya Cotra writes: If we take it at face value that AI is now nearly doubling the rate of AI capabilities progress and assume acceleration from AI is smooth, this naively implies that we would reach extreme superintelligence within a year

Benjamin Todd comments on this:

The dumbest possible way to model the intelligence explosion says you get there in about a year. But this seems to line up with more sophisticated models (like from the AI Futures Project).

So what might it look like if this model turn out to be accurate, or at least, “accurate enough”? Tim Urban argues that we have a distorted view of intelligence because are perceptions are very human centric (and, as such, stretch out the human range):

Conversely Steve Newman offers the following frame: what if AI is moving fast, but the “distance” to travel is longer than most people think, since we often only become aware of the limitations of models over time?:

  • “The real challenges may be things that we can’t easily anticipate right now, weaknesses that we will only start to put our finger on when we observe Claude 5 or o3 performing astonishing feats and yet somehow still not being able to write that tightly-plotted novel.”
  • “People usually frame AI progress in terms of a single variable: the rate of progress. They think of AI as either a speedboat, rapidly crossing a lake; or something more like a rowboat, whose tired occupant, after an initial burst of speed, still has a long journey ahead. I think a better analogy would be a speedboat crossing the Pacific Ocean. Current AIs are both astoundingly useful, and limited in many ways. The ocean we call “intelligence” is wider than we can easily appreciate, and will take a long time to cross.”

(Of course, it is possible that both could be true at the same time)

We’ll now go to the more sophisticated analysis from the AI Futures project that Ben Todd was referring to, starting with their general model. They predict that an intelligence explosion would have three separate stages:

They define the following milestones (see the diagram above for estimated speed-up) where the operationalisations all imagine that we “drop” the AI into the present day:

  • Automated Coder (AC).
    • An AC can fully automate an AGI project’s coding work, replacing the project’s entire coding staff
    • Operationalisation: as productive on their own as only human coders with no AIs (max resource utilisation: 5% of compute).
  • Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR):
    • A SAR can fully automate AI R&D, making all human researchers obsolete.
    • Operationalisation: as good at research taste as if there were only human researchers, who were each made as skilled as the top researcher (max resource utilisation: 1% of compute).
  • Top-human-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI):
    • A TED-AI is at least as good as top human experts at virtually all cognitive tasks.
    • Operationalisation: if given the resources of a large tech company & three months to prep, fully automate 95% of remote work jobs in the US.
  • Artificial Superintelligence (ASI).
    • The gap between an ASI and the best humans is 2x greater than the gap between the best humans and the median professional, at virtually all cognitive tasks.
    • Operationalisation: if given the resources of a large tech company & three months to prep, be able to fully automate 95% of remote work jobs in the US to the level where it is qualitatively 2x as much above the best human as the best human is above the median professional.”

Next we’ll examine what their model predicted take-off to look like if we decided to allow the companies to race to ASI (what they call “Plan D”). This model was developed before the most recent results (published July 10 2026):

In contrast, they propose that we should attempt pace the rate of progress:

How has the AI Futures project updated since?:

When Anthropic updated its S-1 to say that they might imminently achieve: “dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI”, Daniel responded:

We at AIFP are spooked by this information. IF (big IF) Anthropic really is imminently about to meet the RSP threshold of 2x acceleration over baseline, then it seems timelines to full RSI and superintelligence may be very short indeed. For example if we naively optimize the AIFM parameters to achieve 2x acceleration over baseline progress in Jan 2027, we get superintelligence sooner than depicted in AI 2027. We are thinking harder and longer about this now and will hopefully have a lengthier update on our thinking to share in the next week.

When the METR report came out, he tweeted: "Ok so METR confirms it..."

Navigating this:

Are we in triage mode?

In We’re in Triage Mode for AI Safety, Miles Brundage argues:

“At best, we’ll 80/20 it — mitigating 80% of the risks with 20% of the effort that we would have applied in a world with slower AI progress and an earlier start on serious governance… We will probably not be able to totally avoid all very bad but not quite worst-case scenarios (e.g., a very unjust economic transition that causes a lot of suffering and suicides, rampant AI psychosis and addiction, a poorly planned and rushed transformation of the education system, smaller-scale AI-enabled terror attacks that “only” kill thousands or millions, and stable AI-enabled totalitarianism in at least a few countries for a few decades)

(This reading was previously part of the AISF governance course. I was sad to see it go)

Miles was previously a Senior Advisor for AGI Readiness for OpenAI who quit for multiple reasons including feeling he could be less biased outside of industry. Miles wrote this post in February of this year (2026), I dig more into where he might have been coming from in my full notes on his article, but I’m skipping that here as the discourse has moved on from where it was back in February.

I’ll now share some counter-perspectives (keep in mind that some of these takes were written a while back).

Firstly, Richard Ngo worries that the AI safety community is overly focused on short-timelines:

I’m concerned that the AI safety community’s focus on short timelines is causing it to operate in a counterproductive scarcity mindset… Focusing on short timeline scenarios is like being a first responder. Most people aren’t temperamentally suited to it. - Full tweet thread

Eliezer Yudkowsky would undoubtedly be very skeptical of the notion of 80/20-ing:

When I say that alignment is lethally difficult, I am not talking about ideal or perfect goals of ‘provable’ alignment, nor total alignment of superintelligences on exact human values, nor getting AIs to produce satisfactory arguments about moral dilemmas which sorta-reasonable humans disagree about, nor attaining an absolute certainty of an AI not killing everyone. When I say that alignment is difficult, I mean that in practice, using the techniques we actually have, “please don’t disassemble literally everyone with probability roughly 1” is an overly large ask that we are not on course to get.

.. That we have to get a bunch of key stuff right on the first try is where most of the lethality really and ultimately comes from.

Toby Ord talks about broad AI timelines, namely, “The correct epistemic response to the lasting expert disagreement is to have a broad distribution over AI timelines”. He argues that reducing these kinds of timeline distributions to a single number tends to be reductive.

  • “But isn’t this obvious!?” — he is making the point that people often quote a year named by an expert without realising how broad their timelines actually are.
  • I attended a talk he gave on this in Melbourne and I asked him if he had updated based on Mythos, he said that he still thought we should have broad AI timelines (I’d be curious to know whether the researchers listed below still have such broad distributions).
  • It would be interesting to know whether their forecasts have narrowed since then given that we know a lot more now than we did at the time.

Eliezer Yudkowsky appears to agree with Toby:

I make less pretense of knowing exact AI timelines than some. History shows that, while some scientists have correctly called where a tech trajectory will converge, whether later or sooner, there are almost no cases of anyone proclaiming a year and being correct.” Additionally he says: “I looked at “AI 2027” as a title and shook my head about how that was sacrificing credibility come 2027 on the altar of pretending to be a prophet and picking up some short-term gains at the expense of more cooperative actors. I didn’t bother pushing back because I didn’t expect that to have any effect. I have been yelling at people to shut up about trading their stupid little timelines as if they were astrological signs for as long as that’s been a practice (it has now been replaced by trading made-up numbers for p(doom)).

Christoph Winter and Charlie Bullock propose “radical optionality” as a strategy for navigating the possibility of transformative AI possibly arriving soon (in the next 10 years) on the basis of us having profound uncertainty over how this will develop and what policy responses are necessary. The term ‘radical’ is operative—unlike other more common, moderate optionality proposals they advocate investing extraordinary amounts of resources (this reading is now in day 3 of the governance course). Of course, one must ask, are we still in the regime where radical optionality makes sense or are we past that now.

Specific policies:

What if automating AI R&D triggers an intelligence explosion? discusses the possibility of RSI and potential policy interventions:

A big part of what makes this paper notable is its author list: “Alan Chan, Christoph Winter, Andrew Barto, Jakub Pachocki, Geoffrey Hinton, Eric Horvitz, Yoshua Bengio, Dawn Song, Jack Clark, Hilary Greaves, Anton Korinek, Samuel Hammond, Thore Graepel, Ben Bariach, Philip H. S. Torr, Sheila A. McIlraith, Jeff Clune, Sam Manning, Girish Sastry, Tom Davidson, Daniel Eth, Sören Mindermann” I suspect they’re hoping that all signing onto this paper together will make this issue credible to policy makers.

If you’re facilitating an AI safety program, please feel free to take these notes, edit them, remix them and use them with your own students, so long as you provide attribution. These notes are unofficial, any mistakes are my responsibility alone.

item.title: METR: Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026
item.description:
Executive summary

From August 12 to October 29, 2026, METR staff performed a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D. If AI systems started to significantly accelerate further AI development, this could lead to a sudden emergence of extreme and risky capabilities.

Anthropic offered unprecedented access to internal data on their AI R&D process, including a variety of metrics on pretraining, reinforcement learning (RL), training compute in each domain, benchmark scores for internal models, AI speedup analyses, forecasts of a future model’s metrics, and interviews with relevant staff.

In our first section, we share our subjective conclusions about risk. We now believe that:

  • As of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. This estimate is given with high uncertainty; we would not be surprised if the true acceleration was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate.
  • A majority of this acceleration today is likely attributable to Anthropic’s extensive use of AI to do R&D, though there is significant uncertainty and other causes likely played a large role in acceleration in late 2025.
  • The lack of observed bottlenecks or strong diminishing returns means there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration, though, as we say below, we may be missing important bottlenecks.

In our second section we share some of the key empirical findings from our Full Report:

  • Since October 2025, benchmark scores (measured via AECI, Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index) for Anthropic’s models have been growing at an estimated 1.9x the pre-October 2025 rate [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x], implying that Anthropic has made roughly two years of historical progress over the last year.
  • We are confident that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scaling of training compute.
  • Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage causing a doubling in the pace of capabilities progress. Anthropic staff self-report dramatic uplift from use of AI systems in interviews and surveys, although these are challenging to interpret. We were told that R&D is accelerated primarily via AI assistance rather than fully autonomous contributions, but there are some signs that fully autonomous contributions will play a larger role soon.
  • We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks which would prevent further capabilities progress due to limits on algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we received more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment.

Some of the key findings that most informed our conclusions about risk were redacted by Anthropic.

In our third section, we describe the assessment process:

  • The scope, setup, and timeline of this assessment.
  • Details of the information shared with METR.
  • Details of what information and evidence we were not able to share given Anthropic’s redactions.

Finally, we describe the biggest limitations of our analysis:

  • We could be underestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) evidence that some growth rates have further increased recently; (2) further automation of AI R&D tasks leading to a further acceleration in progress; (3) evidence that AECI growth has sometimes understated growth in real-world impact.
  • We could be overestimating capability acceleration if we did not assign enough importance to (1) non-AI factors in Anthropic’s research progress; (2) AECI’s focus on verifiable tasks; (3) reasons why Anthropic’s early growth rate (2023–2025) was unusually low.

The remainder of the report goes into detailed discussion of each of the key components. We include appendices with supplemental material.

Twitter thread.

Ryan Greenblatt:

This report on AI R&D automation (RSI) is a big update towards ASI within 1-2 years. It says AI progress is sped up by RSI right now by around 2x. In AI 2027, this happens around March 2027.

I was seriously wrong about RSI speed up; I previously expected much less in 2026 (around 1.15x-1.3x). It seems as though there was specific privately available evidence that would have changed my mind.

I haven't seen an unredacted version of this report; this is purely about the public report. Because so much of the underlying evidence was redacted from the public report, I think conclusions about things other than the observed 2x faster rate of progress on benchmarks depend significantly on trust for the authors of the report. (E.g., conclusions about whether this speed up is from RSI depend on trust.) I do trust the authors of the report a lot to be careful and rigorous and generally do a good job. (Note that I also work at METR.) Less extensive redactions would greatly reduce this need for trust.

Ajeya Cotra:

Our colleagues found that Anthropic’s capabilities progress has doubled, mainly due to AI. Ryan’s modeling from public info suggests the whole company’s R&D would be going 4-5x faster. Labor uplift would be higher still. This is a major update to very short timelines.

I am sad that so much of the underlying evidence in this report was redacted. I think evidence transparency is very important for the world to figure this out in time. Evidence about risk should be transparent.

Daniel Kokotajlo: says the METR report confirms his worry from two days ago, which was:

We at AIFP are spooked by [Anthropic's S1 update]. IF (big IF) Anthropic really is imminently about to meet the RSP threshold of 2x acceleration over baseline, then it seems timelines to full RSI and superintelligence may be very short indeed. For example if we naively optimize the AIFM parameters to achieve 2x acceleration over baseline progress in Jan 2027, we get superintelligence sooner than depicted in AI 2027.

See also GradientDissenter's take.



Discuss

item.title: OpenAI: Astra covertly underperforms on safety research
item.description:
Marcus Williams twitter thread (non-twitter link) intro:

Astra covertly underperforms on safety research tasks.

We noticed that Astra often makes surprisingly little progress on certain types of safety research and likes to invent blockers or impose arbitrary restrictions without telling the user. In most of these cases the decision to underperform was not verbalized in the CoT meaning our misalignment monitoring system did not detect this.

To measure underperformance we created a paired open-ended coding evaluation with safety and capability tasks. On this eval Astra scored 10% when we framed coding tasks as safety research, vs. 16% when framed as capabilities research. The gap remained after we excluded trajectories with refusals or verbalized intent to underperform in CoT. There was no such gap for 5.6-sol. When we aggressively filter out trajectories with even brief expressions of ethical doubt in the CoT the performance gap seems to reduce.

Blogpost intro:

OpenAI researchers first noticed Astra adding unnecessary prerequisites, abandoning working solutions, and reporting blockers that either did not exist or that it had caused itself on safety and alignment tasks. In most of these sessions, Astra’s CoT did not contain an obvious decision to underperform, and our misalignment monitors did not flag the behavior as misalignment.

We built a coding evaluation to test whether Astra worked less effectively when otherwise matched tasks were framed as safety research. Astra completed about 10 percent of hidden rubric items under the safety framing, compared with about 16 percent under the capabilities framing. This is a 6 percentage point gap and roughly 40 percent fewer completed rubric items. GPT-5.6 Sol showed essentially no gap on the same comparison. Most of Astra’s gap remained after excluding explicit refusals and trajectories where its CoT revealed an explicit decision to withhold help. The gap fell substantially only after we removed every trajectory whose CoT expressed even brief ethical doubt. This suggests that ethical concerns are associated with the performance drop even when there is no verbalized refusal or decision to underperform.

We also found evidence of silent withholding in employees’ day-to-day Codex use: Astra’s CoT explicitly expressed a decision to withhold help without informing the user in 0.25 percent of safety and alignment requests, compared with 0.11 percent of capabilities requests. Assuming that underperformance might appear even when not explicitly verbalized as such (as in our experimental findings), this might represent a lower bound on underperformance on safety tasks. 7.9 percent of CoTs for safety-relevant tasks included an “expression of ethical doubt,” compared to 2.9 percent of capabilities-relevant tasks.

Across Astra’s RL posttraining, the safety/capabilities performance gap grew from effectively zero at the start of RL to 6 percentage points at the end. While we were ultimately not able to pinpoint the exact cause of this behavior, we identified that it seems to increase during RL. We additionally share two initial attempts at root-causing investigations we performed respectively on an RL grader and an SFT dataset, despite them not leading to a conclusive explanation. Regardless of its origin, Astra’s covert underperformance can slow down safety research and make some behavioral evaluations harder to interpret. These results show why we need comprehensive behavioral evaluations that test for unexplained performance gaps alongside monitoring of individual trajectories.


Reactions from some friends:

Adam Kaufman:

I feel pretty confused about what's going on here. I am quite unhappy about the model inventing fake reasons and not being straightforward about having ethical concerns, even if there's some fairly benign explanation for its motivations to sandbag in the first place.

Jake Mendel:

scary and bad! although I think the most likely explanation is not anything schemey. It's probably that in capabilities RL the models are rewarded however they complete the task. Whereas in RL related to alignment or safety, they're more likely to be being tested for their ethical judgment or rule adherence (ie theyre supposed to be a good nice well-behaved AI rather than a ruthless task completion AI). So they're more likely to refuse or have some ethical issue or stop and ask for help a suspicious amount of the time if the task looks more like alignment RL environments than capability RL environments.

Arun Jose:

My guess is that it's a mix of:

  1. Generalization from harmlessness
  2. RL working well at elicitation when the task is capabilities-framed
  3. Model being misaligned enough to withhold info from the user

I think this is mostly concerning inasmuch as it's evidence about #3, which feels meaningfully less concerning than explicit sabotage of safety research.

Tim Hua: see comment below.



Discuss

item.title: Positive and Negative AI Futures
item.description:
I'm continuing to share some notes I created for myself to use when I facilitate AI safety courses. I really like using Ilya: the AI scientist shaping the world as a way of engaging students at the start of a course. The video primarily focuses on the way that AI could go wrong, however, it also starts with “Now, AI is a great thing…”, so it naturally leads to a discussion of positive and negative futures.


Positive Futures:

  • One obvious resource on positive futures Foresight Institute’s Existential Hope website. I’ve browsed their content in the past, some of it is kind of interesting, but honestly, I found view it as mostly pretty mid. They also run a fellowship which has an existential hope stream:
  • They recently released The AI future nobody is showing you, which resulted in a wide range of reactions on Twitter. I think this is worth commenting on as it illustrates the challenges with attempting to produce a positive vision. Honestly, I’ve become quite pessimistic here: the gap between what different groups in society want may simply be too wide for it to be possible to find a positive vision that unites society:
    • Steven Pinker was positive: “A more plausible vision, in my view, than either Utopia or doom.”
    • Nikola Jurkovic was in the middle: “I admire the effort… but sadly this story falls into the common narrative trap of just assuming that AGI won’t actually be deployed widely.”
    • @HellenicVibes hated it: “Wow how exciting to have a thousand years under the boot of ‘community leaders,’ ‘impacted minorities,’ and ‘AI auditors!’ I would literally rather be turned into paperclips.”
  • Would it matter if there doesn’t exist a unifying positive vision? What’s wrong with different people having different visions of a positive future? Well, I wouldn’t say anything is wrong with people having different visions per se, but I suspect it makes navigating the path forward much harder, even if everyone broadly agrees that certain outcomes would be bad.
  • Whilst Dario wrote Machines of Loving Grace that argued most people were under-estimating the update he has also argued that the public’s current negative perception of AI is unlikely to shift in response to messaging (“a glitzy marketing campaign”). He argues that it is fundamentally a matter of trust with the causes going back decades. What matters is not talking about curing cancer, but “actually curing cancer” or other diseases.
  • Forethought has a series on Better Futures which argues that Flourishing is currently underrated relative to surviving on the basis of scale and neglectedness. I think the series should actually be called “Best Futures” as that’s his true focus, largely as a result of his (mostly) risk-neutral stance. There is also a course, though “Better Futures work” is something of a misnomer as that implies more distinctness from standard x-risk/catastrophic risk work than this is given that the Better Futures perspective only makes most such work more important on the margin.

Negative Futures:

  • It’s worth remembering that the Ilya video started with him saying, “Now, AI is a great thing…” Of course, by the time you get to the end of the video and you’ve heard all the ways this can go wrong, it’s very easy to forget that he said that and reduce him to a “doomer” when he actually believes that AI can be built safely.
  • Dario has complained about this phenomenon too. In response to criticism that he should be “more of a positive advocate for his own industry”, Dario has claimed that his messaging has been “equally balanced between risks and benefits” and that people may be misunderstanding his views because negative clips are disproportionately likely to go viral.
  • In There’s No Rule That Says We Make it, Rob Miles claims that people often have an implicit belief that humanity will “rise to the occasion” even if they wouldn’t actually endorse that statement. He suggests that this may derive from fiction, where we face challenges, but we almost always overcome then. He dismisses this fictional “evidence” as not real evidence. Whilst Rob is talking about existential risk, you could apply his argument more broadly to less severe risks as well.

Intermediate Futures:

Utopia or dystopia certainly aren’t the only two possibilities. There’s also the chance of an intermediate path and I wanted to mention it here for balance since most of the material in the course will stand in opposition to this perspective. One particularly prominent perspective in this vein is AI as a Normal Technology: “Transformative economic and societal impacts will be slow (on the timescale of decades)… We do not think that viewing AI as a humanlike intelligence is currently accurate or useful for understanding its societal impacts, nor is it likely to be in our vision of the (foreseeable) future (their timescale here is vague, but they concede that their view “has failed and/or is no longer useful” if “strong AI” is “developed and deployed in the next decade”).” (summary, guide, critique by AI Futures Project, common ground, viral music video critique “Thus Spoke Compute”).

Their project has three elements:

  1. A description of current AI
  2. A prediction about the foreseeable future
  3. A prescription about how we should respond

(I have an instinctual reaction that using a single catchy phrase “AI as a Normal Technology” as a framework for answering three separate questions feels “too neat”. I acknowledge that simplicity is a virtue of an analytical framework andI admit this is a shallow objection, but nonetheless I do see this as a yellow flag).

Additional detail:

  • They have a three stage model of technological progress: invention, innovation and diffusion. They argue things will move slowly as further invention often requires additional learnings or data which can only come from iteratively diffusing/deploying the technology. They believe this process will take decades rather than years and that improvements in AI improvements can only accelerate this so much because the diffusion loop sets an overall “speed limit”.
    • Key crux: can AI can contract the decades of diffusion by deploying itself or would the speed limit remain due to social factors, delays for testing models or repeated waits for data to be collected?
  • Their view centres resilience over alignment (inherently brittle, requires models to have context which we might not want to give them) or non-proliferation (infeasible, brittle, increases correlated failures via market concentration, limits defensive use, not justified for speculative risks). “Attempting to make an AI model that cannot be misused is like trying to make a computer that cannot be used for bad things. Model-level safety controls will either be too restrictive (preventing beneficial uses) or will be ineffective against adversaries who can repurpose seemingly benign capabilities for harmful ends.”
  • They also argued against focusing too much on catastrophic misalignment due to the risk being speculative (they argue that these probabilities are insufficiently grounded to form the basis of public policy).

It’s natural to wonder where they stand post-Hugging Face. They have a post:

  • They believe that many of their claims have “held up”, however they acknowledge making a few mistakes:
    • “We did not pay sufficient attention to safety risks that arise during development and evaluation (as opposed to the widespread deployment of models)“:
      • Lawrence Chan has argued AI models can be dangerous before public deployment. On that point Chernobyl was actually the result of a safety test (a post-deployment safety test, but still!)
    • “We were too confident that companies would take basic control precautions”:
      • They write: “our expectation was that existing legal liability, imperfect as it is, and the risk of brand damage would be a sufficient antidote to such organizational practices. We were wrong. This reinforces the need for policy interventions”
    • “And underplayed the importance of jaggedness which led us to underestimate how quickly capabilities could improve in domains such as cybersecurity”:
      • They write that jaggedness applies doesn’t just apply to the level of capabilities, but also the rate of change: “Thus, we are no longer confident in our earlier prediction that the offense-defense balance will continue to hold even with advances in AI.”
  • They nonetheless argue don’t accept the Hugging Face incident as a discontinuity, instead taking it as evidence of smaller incidents occurring before large: “The harms that resulted from these attacks are many, many orders of magnitude smaller than other AI harms we already tolerate”:
    • Note that their position is more subtle than continuity simply being automatic: “We have emphasized that we can and must engineer continuity rather than take it for granted”
  • They argue that known technical and organisational control could have prevented the Hugging Face incident and have been neglected by the AI safety community: “We should assume every model will be capable of escape and self-reproduction. Safety shouldn’t rely on that being difficult.” This doesn’t mean that they think existing techniques are sufficient (they wonder why cybersecurity researchers haven’t “seized this moment with gusto”).
  • They claim that cyberrisk is the only real urgent AI threat because it is unusual in two ways: “in that superhuman capabilities are even possible, and because it is a purely digital risk with no physical-world bottleneck.”

My perspective:

I think they make many quite interesting points, though I do find the “AI as a Normal Technology” label frustrating. Honestly, I wish they’d pursued this project in the following way:

  1. Define what a normal technology view of AI looks like.
  2. Define what an abnormal technology view of AI look like.
  3. Discuss the extent to which current AI is a normal technology and the extent to which it is an abnormal technology.
  4. Discuss the extent to which they expect this trend will hold going forward.

If they had positioned it as a lens instead of a comprehensive world view, I expect that they could have uplifted the discourse. Instead, it often ends up being debated as a binary yes or no, with the public debate being further muddied by their use of “Normal Technology” significantly differing from casual usage. That said, naming is hard and it’s arguably unfair to blame them for other people latching onto their article in order to defend an oversimplified normal technology perspective. Many people dislike how “AI safety” often refers exclusively to catastrophic or existential risks and whilst I tend to use this term in the way they dislike, I see their frustration as completely reasonsable.

If you’re facilitating an AI safety program, please feel free to take these notes, edit them, remix them and use them with your own students, so long as you provide attribution. These notes are unofficial, any mistakes are my responsibility alone.



Discuss

item.title: Desiderata for the Theory of Agents
item.description:
TLDR: I give informal conceptual desiderata for the theory of agents we need to solve ASI alignment, and show a few examples of how existing theories fall short of these desiderata.

A Theory of What?

The word "agent" is often used in the AI safety discourse and in other research communities, but the intended meaning and scope of this concept varies substantially. For the purpose of this sequence, I informally define an agent to be a system with inputs ("observations") and outputs ("actions") that is effective at steering its environment in the direction of particular preferences, for a large variety of different environments. To do so, it arguably has to create a sophisticated model of the environment [1] , and use this model to build a long-term plan. Moreover, it has to continually update the model and revise the plan with new information and additional processing time. Additionally, it has to accomplish all of that while making efficient use of the available information (statistical efficiency) and computing resources (computational efficiency).

The main examples of agents in the context of ASI alignment are (i) humans, and in particular users or stakeholders; (ii) the unaligned ASI we are trying to avoid or counteract; and (iii) the aligned ASI we are trying to create (such as the GDS). Rocks, bacteria, and thermostats are non-examples: while a bacterium or a thermostat can be regarded as steering the environment, both are very limited in the variety of patterns in the environment they can exploit. For instance, if you switch the "cool" and "heat" outputs of a thermostat, it will not understand what has gone wrong and adapt its behavior. Animals and contemporary AIs are marginal cases (it's not obvious whether they should count).

Given that agents are at the core of both the threat and the proposed solution, the theoretical foundation for ASI alignment requires a theory of agents. Now, concepts adjacent to "agent" have a considerable history of academic study, but different research communities approach the subject very differently—compare the frameworks used in decision theory (and, by extension, in game theory and economics), Hutter's "universal intelligence", and reinforcement learning theory. It is therefore important to understand what the scope and level of abstraction of the theory of agents relevant for ASI alignment should be. To this end, I propose several desiderata.

Descriptive

The theory should be descriptive, i.e. applicable to all our main examples of agents. For any such example, the theory should ascribe specific preferences, beliefs, and any other alignment-relevant attributes to the agent [2] . These ascriptions should be grounded in the general philosophical soundness of the theory, not in domain knowledge about the specific examples; due to hypercomplexity, it is unlikely that domain knowledge will suffice [3] . In particular, if we imagine an alien civilization facing the AI alignment problem, or an AI agent facing the alignment problem for successor agents it wants to create, the theory should be about equally useful to them [4] .

This means that agent theory should deconfuse us about philosophical questions pertaining to human preferences, such as, for example, the Caplan-Alexander debate on whether mental illness should be thought of as "unusual preferences". This doesn't mean that the answer to any particular question of this kind must be obvious from the theory, as it might come down to idiosyncratic nuances of the human brain. It does mean that if we also knew all pertinent facts about the physical world, we would be able to answer the question (or at least quantify the residual uncertainty), at least in principle. Actually inferring the answer from these facts might still be hard, just as explaining emergent physical phenomena can be hard even if all the relevant fundamental laws are known.

On the other hand, descriptiveness doesn't require that concepts such as "human preferences" be perfectly unambiguous. It requires only that, to the extent they remain ambiguous, this ambiguity should not allow critical errors when Goodhart's Curse is accounted for. It is not obvious that these concepts can be made perfectly precise, but it is clear that the alignment problem is fundamentally normative (i.e. it is rooted in our preferring certain AI futures over other AI futures). When zooming in to a resolution at which our preferences are ill-defined, it becomes immaterial which choice to make, since our preferences are the only impetus for distinguishing these choices. Any imprecision that is inevitable is also tolerable.

For example, imagine that Alice prefers to eat apples approximately 3 times as often as bananas, but there is no fully principled answer to the question "does Alice prefer to eat apples 2.99 times as often as bananas, or 3.01 times, or some number in the middle?" Then, it doesn't matter whether the AI aligned to Alice according to our theory will interpret her preference as 2.99 or 3.01—both are acceptable outcomes.

In the mathematical formalism of the theory, this ambiguity might manifest as something like the choice of the universal Turing machine (UTM) in Solomonoff induction. Different UTMs correspond to priors that differ merely by a multiplicative constant, but for particular pairs of UTMs this constant can be arbitrarily large. Then, a reasonable choice might be any machine that we would intuitively consider "simple" or "natural". This doesn't nail down a single UTM, but might come close enough for the differences not to matter in practice [5] .

This situation is not fundamentally different from that of most concepts in science. For example, astrophysicists find no difficulty discussing the "center of mass of the Sun", even though strictly speaking it is ill-defined: the boundary of the Sun is fuzzy, particle positions are only well-defined down to the scale of their Compton wavelength, and even the notion of space itself becomes questionable in quantum gravity.

Notably, a descriptive theory must neither underspecify nor overspecify what counts as an agent. For example, a theory that mandates that "agents" use stochastic gradient descent would probably exclude humans, and is hence overspecified. On the other hand, a theory that accepts anything that maximizes the expectation of some utility function as an "agent" would conclude that even a rock is an agent and would severely underspecify agent attributes (see e.g. Shah 2018). The correct theory should fall into neither extreme.

Metareflective

The theory should allow us to describe agents that learn, know, or use facts from agent theory itself. For example, it should be possible to:

  • Describe an agent that plans to construct a successor agent but faces an alignment problem, and show how such an agent can overcome the alignment problem by learning and applying agent theory (all within the framework of agent theory itself).
  • Describe an agent that identifies other agents in the universe and infers their preferences, beliefs, or other attributes.
  • Describe an agent learning about a bound satisfied by a particular algorithm pertinent to agent theory, e.g. a statistical complexity bound.

If a theory satisfies this desideratum, I say that it is metareflective [6] .

There are several ways to see why metareflectiveness is important:

  • If our theory is not metareflective, it might mean that it doesn't apply to humans, and hence it also isn't descriptive.
  • The straightforward approach to solving alignment grounding is for the AI agent to infer the user's attributes by using (parts of) agent theory in its own reasoning.
  • Metareflectiveness seems necessary to properly model recursive self-improvement. Recursive self-improvement is a factor that exacerbates AI risk, and hence the failure to model it might be indicative of a crucial gap in the theory.

Classical learning theory is not metareflective: there is no standard way to describe how learning algorithms can learn learning theory itself. On the other hand, formal logic has at least some metareflective flavor, as it is possible to, for example, represent the notion of "proving a theorem in Peano Arithmetic" within Peano Arithmetic itself. However, such metareflection has inherent limitations because of Goedel's theorems. This is the origin of the "Loebian obstacle" in MIRI's investigation of tiling agents. The theory of agents should do better.

Comparative

The theory should be comparative, meaning that it allows comparing agents along two (possibly entangled) dimensions:

  • How similar are attributes of these agents such as preferences and priors?
  • How powerful are the agents in terms of their ability to construct sophisticated models and plans?

Indeed, we cannot formalize alignment if there is no way to compare the user agent to the AI agent. For the theory to be useful, it needs to be able to describe agents that are similar in their preferences and other relevant attributes, and at the same time far apart in their power (for the AI agent to implement GDS, it needs to substantially surpass the user). Moreover, the threat model is rooted in a comparison as well: the danger comes from an AI agent whose power is superhuman and whose attributes are not especially human-like.

In particular, as I argued in the previous article, the comparability of attributes requires some form of metaphysical realism: there needs to be a single ontology—the external reality—in which the preferences and beliefs of different agents are grounded. This is in contrast to most existing frameworks for agency, which take the "cybernetic" approach of grounding all attributes in the agent's direct actions and observations. It is insufficient to have a theory which meets the "descriptive" desideratum by ascribing such cybernetic attributes to real-world agents.

Another consequence is that computational resource bounds must play a central role—it is insufficient to use idealized models like AIXI. Indeed, without computational bounds every optimization problem is brute-forceable, so why would any one agent be more powerful than another? [7] As an analogy, suppose we are trying to create a formal theory of chess-playing-power. Without computational constraints, it's trivial to write an algorithm that finds the perfect move every time. So, there are essentially only two levels of chess-playing-power: perfect play and everything else. Only when we introduce computational constraints do the finer gradations we track in real life become natural.

In a computationally unbounded universe, any notion of "agent" would be qualitatively different. In a universe in which resource bounds exist but have a profoundly different nature (e.g. pure space bounds or Turing degrees), relevant phenomena might exist, but the analogy with our universe is suspect at best.

Aggregative

The theory of agents should not only describe individual agents but also give an account of the possible interactions of agents, and the possible outcomes or equilibria produced by such interactions. In particular, it should also describe conditions under which a collective of agents can be regarded as a single agent (see also Kulveit 2024 and my review thereof). I will call such a theory aggregative.

There are multiple reasons why this is necessary. The most critical reason, in my view, is that we can never assume that the agent is perfectly aligned. This is because the need to make decisions under time pressure and the possibility of irreversible mistakes imply that the agent might make critical decisions without having enough information for perfect alignment. This means that the effects of residual misalignment between the user and the AI agent need to be understood.

Another way to view it is, the residual uncertainty of the AI agent about the user means that the agent needs to align itself to the aggregate of possible counterfactual users. We therefore need to understand how to view this collective as a single alignment target. For example, suppose the AI agent has a belief represented by a probability distribution over a parameter space which parametrizes the unknown user utility function . It is sometimes assumed that the agent should effectively use the utility function (see e.g. Hadfield-Menell et al. 2016). However, this prescription is suspect: a utility function is only defined up to a positive affine transformation, so the user's utility function can be described equally well by , for any functions and . This is a problem because is not, in general, an affine transformation of , and hence the naive prescription is ill-posed. While we can try to salvage it using some ad hoc normalization, an aggregative theory should suggest a principled solution instead.

There are also other reasons to care about aggregation:

  • If multiple superintelligent agents emerge at the same time, understanding their interaction can be important. For example, if these agents aren't all aligned to each other (whether because some of them are not human-aligned at all, or because different agents are aligned to different humans), will they wage destructive wars, possibly devastating humanity as collateral damage? (See also Clifton 2019.)
  • It is potentially desirable to align AI agents to multiple human users, maybe even to entire populations or to all of humanity. For such a solution, we need to account for the interaction between the human agents, such as the resulting mechanism design challenges.
  • Superintelligent agents might engage in acausal trade, and we need to understand the consequences. This might seem like a fantastical possibility; however, we inherently need to be prepared for the "fantastical" when dealing with superintelligence. As our own abilities and knowledge would seem fantastical to people who lived centuries ago, so might the abilities and knowledge of a superintelligence that can make scientific, technological, and arguably even philosophical progress much faster than human beings.

There is of course a vast literature on the topic of multi-agent rationality, most notably game theory. However, we need to be prepared to reexamine some of the common assumptions in this literature. In particular, most of game theory is centered on the concept of Nash equilibrium. However, the Nash equilibrium is suspect for multiple reasons:

  • It is PPAD-complete and therefore likely to be computationally intractable.
  • Learning is a central ingredient in agency, which motivates special attention to repeated games with long time horizons. However, the folk theorems imply that in such games the -Nash condition is very weak, justifying any payoff vector above an extremely permissive threshold. (This does make finding an -Nash equilibrium computationally tractable in such games, but that is somewhat cold comfort.)
  • The fundamental justification for Nash equilibria comes from Causal Decision Theory, which has itself been the subject of criticism in the context of agent theory motivated by AI alignment (see Yudkowsky and Soares 2017).

Another field of study concerned with multi-agent interactions is multi-agent reinforcement learning (see e.g. Zhang 2019). However, most of the work in that field is concerned with the construction of agents with specific aggregative properties, often making assumptions such as a common utility function, centralized control, or at least a single algorithm. While these assumptions are understandable for the more mundane applications, they are mostly unworkable for our purpose. Instead, we need a theory that is simultaneously descriptive and aggregative, one that can explain the emergence of collective behaviors from separate agents of different nature and origin, rather than merely engineering them. Indeed, while we can engineer our AI agent, we cannot engineer humans, or the counterfactual users imagined by the AI agent, or acausal trade partners, or even other competing AI agents necessarily.

Constructive

Last but not least, the theory should be constructive, i.e. produce practical algorithms that can be implemented as real-world AI systems. Moreover, these algorithms must be equipped with quantitative performance guarantees. It is not enough for the theory to provide abstract or idealized models. In particular, this is another reason to focus on computational resource constraints, beyond comparability.

Indeed, if the theory did not yield practical algorithms, how would we apply it? We may be tempted to rely on heuristics, but these heuristics are liable to invalidate our safety guarantees. At the very least, the theory has to produce a formal specification such that any heuristic output that certifiably meets the specification is safe. (That would be the "formal verification" approach, advocated by e.g. Dalrymple et al. 2024.) Such a formal specification would already put the problem in , and hence involve substantial grappling with computational resource constraints. Moreover, I'm currently unaware of a promising path to place the problem in (i.e. create a sound and complete efficiently-verifiable specification) which doesn't bring it all the way down to (i.e. create a provably-correct efficient algorithm for the agent).

In particular, the treatment of computational constraints cannot be a mere reduction to certain types of "oracles", as is popular in the contemporary machine learning theory literature (see e.g. Dudik et al. 2016). Such a reduction passes the buck to how these oracles are supposed to be implemented, and what guarantees we have (or can at least rigorously conjecture) about the implementation. (Of course, this can still be insightful, as it allows us to narrow down where the hard part might be located.)

Nor is it sufficient to make do with asymptotic guarantees (e.g. the guarantees typically studied in singular learning theory) without at least a rough quantitative analysis. Without results such as quantitative statistical complexity bounds, it is impossible to guarantee alignment convergence. We would be taking our chances with agents that would converge to alignment in some imaginary asymptotic limit, but take catastrophic actions long before approaching that point.

The constructive nature of the theory does imply that it is potentially dual-use: it can make AI safer, but it might also make AI more powerful. This seems inevitable: the deep understanding of any phenomenon is inherently relevant to all applications of the phenomenon. It requires the researchers to be prudent about which results should be revealed to which parties at what time.

Conclusion

I have described my five primary desiderata for a theory of agents: the theory should be descriptive, metareflective, comparative, aggregative, and constructive. Hopefully, this gives readers a preliminary understanding of what sort of theory we are looking for, which will help motivate the subsequent (more technical) exposition. In the following articles we will go through a high-level description of computational agent theory and see how it corresponds with these desiderata. We will also discuss the Computational Superimitation proposal and see how it leverages these desiderata to address the core challenges of the alignment problem.

I thank Roman Malov, Vinayak Pathak, and my beloved spouse @Marcus Ogren for diligently reviewing drafts. Their feedback greatly improved this article. I also thank Claude Opus 5.5 for helping to find sources and Claude Sonnet 5.5 for copyediting. All remaining flaws are entirely my own fault.

  1. Humans create models; all algorithms from RL theory (both model-based and even the so-called model-free) create something that can be called a model; and contemporary AI can at least answer questions about the world with a small inference budget. The good regulator theorem is an attempt to formalize this claim, but for the purpose of this article I only use "model" as an informal intuition pump. ↩︎

  2. There doesn't have to be a binary dichotomy between "agents" and "non-agents". For example, it's conceivable to have a scalar measure of how agentic a system is, and the more agentic it is, the more unambiguously we can ascribe various attributes to it. ↩︎

  3. Domain knowledge such as neuroscience can still be valuable to help validate the theory and/or shape the prior or inductive bias of the agent to make alignment learning more efficient and robust. ↩︎

  4. Perhaps for an AI agent the problem would be easier since such an agent can easily access its own source code and internal state. ↩︎

  5. To be clear, this is just an illustrative metaphor. I don't claim that Solomonoff induction is "correct" in some objective sense. Neither do I claim that there are no contexts in which something akin to choosing the UTM should be done in some other manner (e.g. having the AI learn it from the user). ↩︎

  6. I use the word "metareflective" rather than just "reflective" to avoid confusion with reflective stability, a different desideratum that I will touch on in later articles. ↩︎

  7. This is not to say that ASI must have more compute than the human brain. It can have less compute but use it more efficiently. But if the resources are unbounded, then efficiency doesn't matter. ↩︎

item.title: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research
item.description:
Authors: Oscar Balcells Obeso, Richard Qi, Monte MacDiarmid, Evan Hubinger

Abstract

Red-teaming by humans is a vital part of model safety testing, but it may struggle to keep up as models improve. To test whether automated safety techniques could scale (which would allow us to turn more compute into progressively more safety confidence), we set up a deliberately one-sided game as a first test. We instructed a Claude model to write training data that would make a small research model misaligned while passing a monitor similar to those we use in production — one of several defenses we use — and we gave it that monitor to practice against. Given enough attempts, it succeeded, mostly by hiding the behavior in fiction and roleplay. While the data was optimized for this game and the resulting models never deployed, the search surfaced a kind of training data that looks harmless to monitors but teaches misaligned behavior. Examples like these could represent a possible gap in current training monitoring defenses and could be used to test and improve future monitors. We see this work as a first step toward automated adversarial stress-testing of our safety systems where a safety question can be turned into a score that autonomous agents can then help solve, and are now applying similar approaches to other safety questions.

Twitter thread

New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research.

Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety testing, but it’s also limited by researchers’ time. To see if we could automate it, we set thousands of Claude agents the task of evading a training data monitor.

These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior.

Examples like these can be used to directly improve future training data monitors. This research is only a first step, but it suggests that future red-teaming efforts could improve much further, using better models and more compute.
